butir.teks: Al-Hasan said: Among those before you was a man who had precedence in Islam and companionship with the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him). 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak said: By this he meant Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas (may Allah be pleased with him). He said: He would not frequent the rulers and would shun them. His sons said to him, "These people are visited by those who are not like you in companionship and precedence in Islam, so if only you would go to them." He said, "My sons, shall I go to a carcass around which a people have gathered? By Allah, if I am able, I will not share it with them." They said, "Father, then we will perish from emaciation." He said, "My sons, to die a thin believer is dearer to me than to die a fat hypocrite." Al-Hasan said: By Allah, he got the better of them in argument, since he knew that the earth eats flesh and fat but not faith.
In this is an indication that one who enters upon the ruler is never free from hypocrisy at all, and it is the opposite of faith.

Abu Dharr said to Salama, "Salama, do not frequent the doors of the rulers, for you will not obtain anything of their worldly goods except that they will obtain from your religion something better than it."

This is a great trial for the scholars and a hard pretext for Satan against them, especially one who has an acceptable manner of speaking and sweet words. For Satan keeps suggesting to him that in your admonishing them and your entering upon them there is what will restrain them from wrongdoing and establish the rites of the law, until it is made to appear to him that entering upon them is part of the religion. Then, once he has entered, he does not delay in softening his speech, flattering, and plunging into praise and extolment, and in this lies the ruin of religion.

It used to be said: When scholars know, they act; when they act, they are kept busy; when they are kept busy, they are missed; when they are missed, they are sought; and when they are sought, they flee. 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz (may Allah have mercy on him) wrote to al-Hasan: To proceed: advise me of people whom I may take as helpers in the matter of Allah Most High. He wrote back to him: As for the people of religion, they do not want you; as for the people of this world, you will not want them; but you should take the nobles, for they guard their nobility from defiling it with betrayal.

This concerns 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz (may Allah have mercy on him), and he was the most renunciant of the people of his time. If the condition for the people of religion is to flee from him, how then can seeking out others and mixing with them be deemed fitting? The early scholars of the salaf, such as al-Hasan, ath-Thawri, Ibn al-Mubarak, al-Fudayl, Ibrahim ibn Adham, and Yusuf ibn Asbat, never ceased to speak against the scholars of this world among the people of Mecca, Syria, and elsewhere, either because of their inclination to this world or because of their mixing with the rulers. Among them is that he not be hasty toward giving legal opinions, but rather be hesitant and cautious for as long as he finds a way to deliverance.

If he is asked about what he knows with certainty by the explicit text of the Book of Allah, or by an explicit text of a hadith, or by consensus (ijma'), or by clear analogy (qiyas), he gives a legal opinion. If he is asked about what he doubts, he says, "I do not know." If he is asked about what he thinks by means of ijtihad and conjecture, he is cautious, excuses himself, and refers the matter to someone else, if there is sufficiency in someone else. This is prudence, because taking on the risk of ijtihad is great. In the report: "Knowledge is three: a speaking Book, an established Sunna, and 'I do not know.'" (١) Ash-Sha'bi said: "I do not know" is half of knowledge.

Whoever keeps silent where he does not know, for the sake of Allah Most High, is no less in reward than one who speaks, because admitting ignorance is harder on the self. Such was the habit of the Companions and the early generations (salaf) (may Allah be pleased with them).

Ibn 'Umar, when asked for a legal opinion, would say, "Go to this ruler who has taken on the affairs of the people and put it around his neck." Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said, "He who gives legal opinions to the people on everything they ask him about is mad." And he said, "The shield of the scholar is 'I do not know'; if he misses it, his vital spots have been struck."

Ibrahim ibn Adham (may Allah have mercy on him) said: Nothing is harder on Satan than a scholar who speaks with knowledge and is silent with knowledge. He says, "Look at this one: his silence is harder on me than his speech."

One of them described the substitutes (abdal) and said: Their eating is out of need, their sleep is by being overcome, and their speech is out of necessity. That is, they do not speak until they are asked; and if they are asked and find someone who will suffice them, they remain silent; and if they are compelled, they answer. They used to count beginning to speak before being asked as a hidden appetite for speech.
'Ali and 'Abd Allah (may Allah be pleased with them both) passed by a man who was speaking to the people, and he said, "This one is saying, 'Know me.'"
One of them said: The scholar is only the one who, when asked about a question, is as though his molar were being pulled out.
Ibn 'Umar used to say, "You want
to make us a bridge on which you cross over us to Hell."

Abu Hafs an-Naysaburi said: The scholar is the one who, when asked, fears that it will be said to him on the Day of Resurrection, "From where did you answer?" Ibrahim at-Taymi, when asked about a question, would weep and say, "Did you find no one but me, so that you came to need me?"
Abu al-'Aliya ar-Riyahi, Ibrahim ibn Adham, and ath-Thawri used to speak to two, three, or a small group, and when they became many, they left.

The Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said: "I do not know whether 'Uzayr was a prophet or not, nor do I know whether Tubba' was cursed or not, nor do I know whether Dhu al-Qarnayn was a prophet or not." (١) When the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) was asked about the best and the worst places on earth, he said, "I do not know," until Gabriel (peace be upon him) came down to him and he asked him, and he said, "I do not know," until Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, informed him that the best places are the mosques and the worst are the markets. (٢) Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) would be asked ten questions, would answer one, and would stay silent about nine, whereas Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) would answer nine and stay silent about one.
Among the jurists were those who said "I do not know" more often than they said "I know": among them Sufyan ath-Thawri, Malik ibn Anas, Ahmad ibn Hanbal, al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad, and Bishr ibn al-Harith.

'Abd ar-Rahman ibn Abi Layla said: In this mosque I met one hundred and twenty of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him); none of them was asked about a hadith or a legal opinion without wishing that his brother would suffice him in that.

In another wording: A question would be presented to one of them, and he would refer it to another, and the other would refer it to another, until it came back to the first. It is reported that a roasted head was given as a gift to one of the People of the Suffa, while he was in extreme hardship, and he gave it as a gift to another, and the other gave it to another, and so it went around among them until it returned to the first.

Now see how the matter of the scholars has been reversed, so that what was fled from has become sought, and what was sought has become fled from. Evidence for the goodness of caution against taking on legal opinions is what was reported with a chain of transmission from one of them, that he said: "None gives legal opinions to the people except three: a ruler, one commissioned, or one who imposes himself."
Some of them said: The Companions used to push four things off onto one another: leadership, the bequest, the deposit, and the legal opinion.
Some of them said: The quickest of them to give legal opinions was the least in knowledge, and the most firm in pushing it away was the most scrupulous of them.

The occupation of the Companions and the Followers (tabi'un) (may Allah be pleased with them) was in five things: reciting the Qur'an, maintaining the mosques, remembrance (dhikr) of Allah Most High, enjoining the right, and forbidding the wrong. That was because of what they had heard from his saying (peace and blessings be upon him), "All the speech of the son of Adam is against him and not for him, except three: a command to do right, a prohibition of wrong, or the remembrance of Allah Most High." (٣) And Allah Most High said, ⟦QS 4:114⟧ the verse.

One of the scholars saw in a dream one of the people of personal opinion from among the people of Kufa and said, "How did you find what you were engaged in of legal opinions and personal opinion?" He scowled and turned away from him and said, "We found it to be nothing, and we did not praise its outcome."
Ibn Husayn said: One of them gives a legal opinion on a question which, had it come before 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), he would have gathered the veterans of Badr for it.
Silence never ceased to be the habit of the people of knowledge, except in necessity.

In the hadith: "When you see a man who has been given silence and renunciation, draw near to him, for he is taught wisdom." (٤) It was said: The scholar is either a scholar of the common people, who is the mufti, and they are the associates of the rulers, or a scholar of the elite, who is the one knowledgeable in the affirmation of Divine oneness (tawhid) and the works of the hearts, and they are the people of the corners, scattered and solitary.
It used to be said: Ahmad ibn Hanbal is like the Tigris, from which everyone scoops; and Bishr ibn al-Harith is like a sweet well, covered, which is sought out only by one person after another.
They used to say, "So-and-so is a scholar,"

and so-and-so is a theologian, and so-and-so speaks more, and so-and-so does more. Abu Sulayman said: Knowledge of Allah (ma'rifa) is nearer to silence than to speech. It was said: When knowledge increases, speech decreases, and when speech increases, knowledge decreases. Salman wrote to Abu ad-Darda' (may Allah be pleased with them both), the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) having made them brothers (١): "My brother, it has reached me that you have sat down as a physician treating the sick. So consider: if you are a true physician, then speak, for your speech is a cure; but if you are one who only pretends to be a physician, then fear Allah, fear Allah, and do not kill
a Muslim." After that Abu ad-Darda' would hold back when asked. Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), when asked, would say, "Ask our mawla al-Hasan."
Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both), when asked, would say, "Ask Haritha ibn Zayd." Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both) would say, "Ask Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab."

It is related that a Companion narrated twenty hadiths in the presence of al-Hasan and was asked about their explanation. He said, "I have nothing but what I narrated." So al-Hasan began explaining them, hadith by hadith, and they marveled at the excellence of his explanation and his memory. Then the Companion took a handful of pebbles and threw them at them and said, "You ask me about knowledge, while this learned scholar is in your midst!"

Among them is that most of his concern be with the knowledge of the inner, vigilance over the heart (muraqaba), knowledge of the path of the Hereafter and walking it, and sincere hope for the unveiling of that through spiritual struggle (mujahada) and vigilance. For spiritual struggle leads to witnessing (mushahada), and through it the subtleties of the knowledge of the heart cause springs of wisdom to burst forth from the heart. As for books and teaching, they do not suffice for that; rather, wisdom, which is beyond limit and count, opens only through spiritual struggle, vigilance, engaging in the outward and inward works, sitting with Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in solitude with presence of the heart in pure reflection, and cutting oneself off to Allah Most High from all else. That is the key of inspiration and the source of unveiling. How many a learner has studied for a long time and yet has been unable to go beyond what he heard by a single word; and how many one who limited himself to what was essential in learning and devoted himself to action and vigilance over the heart, and Allah opened for him such subtleties of wisdom as bewilder the minds of people of understanding. For that reason the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) said, "Whoever acts on what he knows, Allah makes him inherit the knowledge of what he does not know." (٢)

How many subtle meanings among the secrets of the Qur'an cross the hearts of those wholly devoted to remembrance and reflection, which the books of exegesis (tafsir) lack and which the most excellent exegetes have not come upon. When that is unveiled to the vigilant aspirant (murid) and is presented to the exegetes, they approve it and know that it is among the awakenings of pure hearts and the kindnesses of Allah Most High to lofty aspirations turned toward Him.
